html:
The Gitxsan are an Indigenous people of the upper Skeena River in northern British Columbia. Lax̱yip means their territories. They speak a Tsimshianic language, close to that of the Nisga'a and related to Tsimshian on the coast.

Their land is held by houses, large family groups that own fishing sites and hunting grounds. Each house has chiefs, crests and stories, shown on carved totem poles and confirmed at feasts like the potlatch. Salmon from the Skeena was the base of life.

Fur traders and then settlers arrived in the 1800s, and Canada banned the potlatch from 1885 to 1951. Together with their neighbours the Wet'suwet'en, the Gitxsan took their land claim to court. The case, Delgamuukw v. British Columbia, ended in 1997 with a Supreme Court ruling that Aboriginal title still exists in Canada and that oral histories count as evidence.
